title: Choose a Direction, Not a Goal
subtitle: A four-minute values reflection can turn a vague dilemma into one small, chosen action—without requiring a perfect answer or a change of mood.
imageAlt: Two adult friends sit at a kitchen table, each writing privately in a notebook before deciding whether to share.
imageConcept: Two adult siblings or close friends at a lived-in kitchen table, daylight across two open notebooks and mugs; one writes while the other looks down at their own page, leaving space for private reflection and optional conversation.
body: A different question for a stuck moment

When a decision feels tangled, the first instinct is often to ask how to make the discomfort stop or which choice will produce the best result. A values reflection asks something quieter: what quality do you want to bring to this particular moment? Perhaps you want to be honest in a difficult conversation, patient while a decision takes time, curious about a disagreement, or caring toward someone without taking over their problem.

The aim is not to find a grand purpose or uncover a hidden, definitive self. It is to name a direction that matters here, then identify one action that could express it. Values work in behavior-analytic approaches is often described in terms of chosen directions and the actions that can move toward them; a direction is different from a finish line [1]. That distinction makes the exercise useful even when the outcome is uncertain.
A direction is not a destination

A goal is something you can complete: send the email, attend the appointment, resolve the dispute. A value is a quality you can bring to more than one situation: clarity, respect, generosity, independence, or learning. Goals can be useful, but they depend on circumstances and other people. A chosen quality can guide your next move even when you cannot control what happens afterward.

Imagine you are considering whether to raise a concern with a friend. “Make them understand” is an outcome, not a direction; it depends on their response. “Be honest” might point toward saying what has been bothering you without exaggerating or accusing. “Be kind” might suggest choosing a private moment and leaving room for their perspective. Neither value dictates a single correct script. The useful question is what you want to stand for in the exchange, not how to guarantee its result.
Four minutes, with no special technique

Set a timer if a short boundary helps, or simply move through the questions at your own pace. Sit, stand, or walk somewhere you can pause safely. There is no required breathing pattern, posture, or mood to achieve. The exercise is about direction, not relaxation.

First, describe the situation in one plain sentence: “I have not answered the message about the weekend,” or “I need to decide whether to ask for help.” Try to state what is happening without adding a verdict about yourself. Next ask, “What quality do I want to bring to this?” Choose a word that feels relevant—not impressive. Then ask, “What is one small action that would express it here?” A short message, a question, or a decision to wait until you can speak privately may all count. The whole reflection can fit on a scrap of paper.
Make the action observable and small

An action is easier to use when you could point to it afterward. “Be more confident” is difficult to observe and can turn into a demand to feel different. “Write down the question I want to ask” is concrete. “Be a better sibling” is broad and loaded; “ask whether my sister wants advice or just company” is a specific way to express care.

Keep the action modest enough that it remains yours to choose. It might be to read a form before replying, admit that you need more time, ask one curious question, or decline a request with a clear sentence. It need not solve the situation or display the value perfectly. A small action is not a lesser version of a life-changing breakthrough; it is simply the next available expression of a chosen direction. If the situation is beyond your control, look for an action within it that is.
Notice when a value turns into a “should”

Reflection can become another scorecard. You might write “selfless” because that sounds admirable, although what you actually need is a boundary. You might choose “forgiving” because someone expects it, not because it is the direction you want to take. Values work may involve socially desirable responding and aversive private events; these are considerations in implementing values approaches [2].

If a word arrives with pressure or self-criticism, pause and ask whose standard it represents. You can try another word, make the action smaller, or stop without completing anything. Sometimes the honest answer is “I don’t know yet.” That is a valid stopping place, not evidence that you failed the exercise. You do not have to share what you wrote, defend your choice, or prove that a value is important enough.
Use it to orient, not to diagnose

Values reflection is a practical prompt, not a treatment plan or a promise of relief. Research on the valuing process in Acceptance and Commitment Therapy has found that available measures are limited and inconsistent in the constructs they assess [3]. A four-minute reflection cannot establish what someone should do, predict how a conversation will go, or guarantee a better mood. Its modest use is to help connect what matters to a concrete next action.

That modesty matters when the situation involves risk, coercion, serious distress, or a decision that needs specialist advice. A value such as courage does not require staying in an unsafe conversation. Care does not mean taking responsibility for another adult’s choices. If the reflection makes the situation feel harder, set it aside and seek support that fits the need. The exercise should serve your judgment, not replace it.

If you try the reflection with a friend or family member, each person can write privately first. Then, only if both want to, share one chosen quality and one possible action. The listener’s job is not to assign a value, correct the answer, or turn the conversation into a plan. A simple “Would you like me to listen, or help you think it through?” leaves the other person in charge of what happens next.

A shared setting can be useful because people often face the same event from different positions. Two siblings planning a visit might choose connection and reliability, yet arrive at different actions: one could suggest a time to call; the other might be clear about what they can manage. Different choices do not mean one person cares more. If talking starts to feel like pressure, return to private writing or stop. The reflection belongs to the person doing it.
Let the next move stay yours

Try this once with a real, manageable decision—not the most painful or urgent one in your life. Write the situation in one sentence, choose a quality you genuinely want to bring, and name an action small enough to do or decline. For the friends at the kitchen table, that could mean each person privately writing before deciding whether to share. When the timer ends, fold the page or leave it open; there is no need to report back or turn it into a promise. Later, you can ask only: did this action fit the direction I chose, or would I choose differently now? The answer can change as the situation changes.
